anchor: A Chieftain to the Highlands bound
note: Chieftain: the head of a Scottish clan. The Highlands are the mountainous north of Scotland.

anchor: Boatman, do not tarry!
note: Tarry: to delay or linger.

anchor: To row us o’er the ferry
note: Ferry: a boat that carries people across water, or the crossing itself.

anchor: My blood would stain the heather
note: Heather: a low shrub that covers Scottish hills and moors.

anchor: Then who will cheer my bonny bride
note: Bonny: pretty and pleasant, a Scottish word.

anchor: Out spoke the hardy Highland wight
note: Wight: a person, a fellow. Hardy: tough and brave.

anchor: But for your winsome lady
note: Winsome: charming and engaging, pleasing to look at.

anchor: By this the storm grew loud apace
note: Apace: quickly, at a rapid pace.

anchor: The water-wraith was shrieking
note: Water-wraith: a ghost or spirit of the water, whose cry was thought to foretell drowning.

anchor: And in the scowl of heaven each face
note: Scowl: a dark, angry frown.

anchor: And as the night grew drearer
note: Drearer: more gloomy and dismal.

anchor: Adown the glen rode armed men
note: Adown: down. Glen: a narrow valley.

anchor: Though tempests round us gather
note: Tempests: violent storms. The lady says she fears her father more.

anchor: And still they row’d amidst the roar
note: Row’d: rowed. The poet shortens the word to fit the meter.

anchor: Of waters fast prevailing
note: Prevailing: gaining strength and winning out over the boat.

anchor: His wrath was changed to wailing
note: Wrath: fierce anger. Wailing: loud crying from grief.

anchor: For, sore dismay’d
note: Sore: very much, painfully. Dismay’d: struck with fear.

anchor: ’Twas vain: the loud waves lash’d the shore
note: Vain: useless. His call came too late and could not be heard.

anchor: How delicious is the winning
note: Winning: gaining the love and favor of someone.

anchor: For the knot there’s no untying
note: The knot is marriage, which a popular phrase calls a bond one cannot undo.

anchor: ’midst your wooing
note: Wooing: courting, trying to win someone’s love.

anchor: Love has bliss, but Love has ruing
note: Ruing: sorrow, regret, feeling sorry afterward.

anchor: Other smiles may make you fickle
note: Fickle: changeable, not loyal. New smiles can turn a lover’s heart.

anchor: Longest stays, when sorest chidden
note: Chidden: scolded, rebuked with angry words.

anchor: Bind the aspen ne’er to quiver
note: Aspen: a poplar tree whose leaves tremble in the slightest breeze.

anchor: Then bind Love to last for ever
note: The poet lists impossible tasks to show that love cannot be held fixed.

anchor: Love’s wing moults when caged and captured
note: Moults: sheds feathers, as birds do.

anchor: Only free, he soars enraptured
note: Enraptured: filled with delight. Love is happy only when free.

anchor: Can you keep the bee from ranging
note: Ranging: roaming widely. A bee, like love, cannot be kept in one place.

anchor: Or the ringdove’s neck from changing
note: Ringdove: a wood pigeon whose neck feathers change color in the light.

anchor: Gem of the crimson-colour’d Even
note: Even: evening. Crimson: deep red, here the color of the sunset.

anchor: Companion of retiring day
note: Retiring: withdrawing, going to rest.

anchor: So fair thy pensile beauty burns
note: Pensile: hanging down, as the evening star hangs low in the sky.

anchor: So due thy plighted love returns
note: Plighted: pledged or promised. The star’s return each evening is like a promise kept.

anchor: Sure some enamour’d orb above
note: Enamour’d: in love. Orb: a heavenly body, a star or planet.

anchor: Thine is the breathing, blushing hour
note: The hour of dusk, when light fades pink and the evening air seems to breathe.

anchor: Of Love’s delicious witchery
note: Witchery: charm that seems magical.

anchor: Queen of propitious stars, appear
note: Propitious: favorable, bringing good luck.

anchor: And wanton flowers
note: Wanton: growing freely and luxuriantly.

anchor: Embalms the soft exhaling dew
note: Embalms: fills with fragrance. Exhaling: giving off vapor.

anchor: Where dying winds a sigh bequeath
note: Bequeath: to pass on or leave to another.

anchor: Where, winnow’d by the gentle air
note: Winnow’d: blown through, stirred by a current of air.

anchor: Her silken tresses darkly flow
note: Tresses: long locks of hair.

anchor: In converse sweet to wander far
note: Converse: conversation, talk. The speaker pictures strolling and talking with Caroline.

anchor: And she look’d on her lover
note: Ellen’s bower is her private room in the castle.

anchor: Though her smile on him was dwelling
note: She smiles at him, but he does not recognize her, she is so pale.

anchor: Nor love’s own kiss shall wake those eyes
note: She has died, and not even love can wake her.

anchor: The spirits of your fathers
note: The poem recalls earlier British sailors who died at sea.

anchor: Where Blake and mighty Nelson fell
note: Robert Blake and Horatio Nelson were great British admirals. Nelson fell in battle, and the song calls on sailors to follow them.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Blake, Robert”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Blake%2C_Robert; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Nelson, Horatio Nelson, Viscount”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nelson%2C_Horatio_Nelson%2C_Viscount

anchor: Britannia needs no bulwarks
note: Bulwarks: walls built for defense. Britannia is a name and picture of Britain as a woman.

anchor: With thunders from her native oak
note: British warships were built of oak, and the thunder is the sound of their guns.

anchor: The meteor flag of England
note: Meteor: a bright streak across the sky. The flag is pictured as a blazing light.

anchor: Of Nelson and the North
note: In 1801 Nelson led a British fleet against the Danish fleet at Copenhagen, after Denmark and other northern powers joined a league against Britain.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Copenhagen”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Copenhagen; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Nelson, Horatio Nelson, Viscount”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nelson%2C_Horatio_Nelson%2C_Viscount

anchor: Sing the glorious day’s renown
note: Renown: fame, wide honor. The poem opens by praising the day of Nelson’s victory.

anchor: All the might of Denmark’s crown
note: In 1801 the British fleet attacked Denmark’s fleet at Copenhagen after the northern powers formed an armed league against British trade at sea.

anchor: By each gun the lighted brand
note: Brand: a burning piece of wood, here a match lit to fire cannon.

anchor: Like leviathans afloat
note: Leviathan: a huge sea monster, here a mighty warship.

anchor: While the sign of battle flew
note: Flags on the British ships signaled the order to fight.

anchor: It was ten of April morn by the chime
note: The Battle of Copenhagen was fought on the 2nd of April 1801, when the Danes resisted bravely but lost their fleet.

anchor: But the might of England flush’d
note: Flush’d: glowed with excitement and eagerness.

anchor: And her van the fleeter rush’d
note: Van: the front part of a fleet or army.

anchor: “Hearts of oak!” our captains cried
note: Hearts of oak: a phrase for brave sailors. Ships of oak and men of oak.

anchor: From its adamantine lips
note: Adamantine: unbreakable, hard as diamond. The “lips” are the cannon’s mouth.

anchor: Spread a death-shade round the ships
note: Cannon smoke covers the ships like the shadow of a solar eclipse.

anchor: And the havoc did not slack
note: Havoc: widespread destruction. Slack: grow less intense.

anchor: As they strike the shatter’d sail
note: To strike a sail or flag is to lower it as a sign of surrender.

anchor: Or in conflagration pale
note: Conflagration: a large destructive fire, here of burning ships.

anchor: And make submission meet
note: Meet: fitting, proper. Nelson asks the Danes to yield in a fitting way.

anchor: Full many a fathom deep
note: Fathom: a measure of water depth, six feet.

anchor: Elsinore!
note: Elsinore is a Danish town on the narrowest part of the Sound, the strait between Denmark and Sweden.

anchor: With the gallant good Riou
note: Captain Edward Riou led a squadron of frigates at Copenhagen in 1801, fighting beside Nelson’s division, and was killed there.

anchor: And the mermaid’s song condoles
note: Condoles: expresses sympathy with the grieving.

anchor: On Linden, when the sun was low
note: The Battle of Hohenlinden was fought on 2 December 1800 near Munich. French troops under Moreau beat the Austrians. Hohen Linden means “high lime trees.”
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 215, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: All bloodless lay the untrodden snow
note: The snow is white and untouched before the battle begins.

anchor: Commanding fires of death to light
note: The drum calls the army to light its guns and torches.

anchor: Each horseman drew his battle-blade
note: Blade: sword. Each horseman draws his sword for the coming battle.

anchor: And furious every charger neigh’d
note: Charger: a horse trained for battle.

anchor: To join the dreadful revelry
note: Revelry: noisy merrymaking. The poet calls the battle a dreadful party.

anchor: Then shook the hills with thunder riven
note: Riven: split apart. The hills are split with the thunder of guns.

anchor: Far flash’d the red artillery
note: Artillery: large guns. The cannon flash red in the dark.

anchor: Can pierce the war-clouds, rolling dun
note: Dun: dull grayish-brown, the color of the battle smoke.

anchor: Shout in their sulphurous canopy
note: Sulphurous: smelling of sulfur, from burning gunpowder. Canopy: the overhead cover of smoke.

anchor: And charge with all thy chivalry
note: Chivalry: mounted knights, here Bavarian horsemen.

anchor: The snow shall be their winding-sheet
note: Winding-sheet: the cloth wrapped around a dead body.

anchor: Shall be a soldier’s sepulchre
note: Sepulchre: a tomb. Every patch of turf becomes a soldier’s grave.

anchor: When first the fiery mantled Sun
note: Mantled: cloaked, covered as with a cloak.

anchor: His heavenly race began to run
note: The sun runs a race across the sky, and his children the Seasons fly around the earth.

anchor: First, in green apparel dancing
note: Apparel: clothing. Spring is dressed in green leaves.

anchor: Her bright-hair’d sire
note: Sire: father, here the sun.

anchor: On Calpe’s olive-shaded steep
note: Calpe is the old name for Gibraltar, the great rock at the southern tip of Spain, at the entrance to the Mediterranean.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 256, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Or India’s citron-cover’d isles
note: Citron: a lemonlike fruit, here growing on warm islands.

anchor: More remote and buxom-brown
note: Buxom: plump and healthy, here full of vigor.

anchor: A rich pomegranate gemm’d her crown
note: The pomegranate is a fruit with many red seeds, ripe in autumn.

anchor: To hills that prop the polar star
note: Winter flees to the far north, whose hills seem to hold up the pole star.

anchor: Round the shore where loud Lofoden
note: Lofoden is a group of islands off northwest Norway, where a great whirlpool, the Maelstrom, was said to swallow whales.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 256, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Round the hall where Runic Odin
note: Odin was the chief god of the northern peoples, worshiped chiefly by warriors. The poem borrows his northern mythology for Winter’s hall.

anchor: Deflowering Nature’s grassy robe
note: Deflowering: stripping of flowers. Winter strips the earth of its flowers.

anchor: The Lapland drum delights to hear
note: Lapland is the far-northern region of Europe, here named for the cold of its winters.

anchor: Thy horror-breathing agues cease to lend
note: Agues: fevers with chills. Winter is asked to spare the poor.

anchor: The sailor on his airy shrouds
note: Shrouds: ropes that brace a ship’s mast.

anchor: Star that bringest home the bee
note: Bringest: brings. Old second-person verb form.

anchor: And sett’st the weary labourer free
note: Sett’st: set, the old second-person verb form. The evening star ends the workday.

anchor: Whilst far-off lowing herds are heard
note: Lowing: the deep sound cattle make.

anchor: Their remembrancer in Heaven
note: Remembrancer: one who reminds others of something.

anchor: Our bugles sang truce
note: Truce: a pause in fighting.

anchor: And the sentinel stars set their watch in the sky
note: Sentinel: a guard. The stars are pictured as guards on duty.

anchor: By the wolf-scaring faggot that guarded the slain
note: Faggot: a bundle of sticks used as fuel for a fire.

anchor: Methought from the battle-field’s dreadful array
note: Methought: it seemed to me.

anchor: And fain was their war-broken soldier to stay
note: Fain: gladly, willing. The soldier is glad to stay, but dawn ends the dream.

anchor: The gladsome current of our youth
note: Gladsome: cheerful and joyful, as the stream of youth is.

anchor: And life itself is vapid
note: Vapid: dull, without interest or spirit.

anchor: Indemnifying fleetness
note: Indemnifying: making up for a loss. The speed of old age pays back the slow years of youth.
